FOR MARKETING TEAMS
The launch date is locked. The press release is written. The ads are approved and ready to go.
And the page they all point to? Still "in the queue."

If you run marketing for a growing business, you know this feeling. The campaign is ready. The page isn't. And every day it sits in someone else's backlog is a day your budget, your timing and your momentum quietly slip away.

This post is for marketing managers, in-house marketing teams and business owners who need one great page live, fast. Not a new website. Not a six-month rebuild. Just one custom, on-brand page that does one job really well.
Let's talk about why that page is so hard to get, and how to get it anyway.

Your main website was built to do a lot of things at once. Explain who you are. List your services. House your team bios, your blog, your careers page and that PDF from 2021 nobody can find the source file for.
That's its job. And it's a good job.
But a campaign has a different job. A campaign needs focus. One message. One audience. One action.
When you drop a campaign into your main site, a few things tend to happen:
It gets diluted. Visitors land on your campaign page and immediately see your full navigation, your footer links and six other places to click. Attention leaks everywhere.
It has to follow the old rules. Your main site's templates were designed years ago for a different purpose. Your new campaign creative gets squeezed into layouts that were never meant for it.
It triggers a bigger conversation. Suddenly it's not "can we add a page?" It's "who owns the CMS?" and "does this need legal review?" and "should we just redo the whole site while we're in there?"
A standalone landing page sidesteps all of that. It lives on its own, on a subdomain or a separate domain, and it's built around one thing: the campaign.
Here's the honest reason most campaign pages launch late, look off-brand or never happen at all.
The people who can build them are busy.
If you have an in-house web team, they're buried in platform work, bug fixes and the product roadmap. Your landing page is a "nice to have" sitting behind a dozen "must haves."

If you work with an agency, a single landing page is often too small to get their best people on it and too big to turn around quickly. You get a scope document, a kickoff in three weeks and an invoice that makes your finance lead ask questions.

If you try to do it yourself with a drag-and-drop page builder, you end up with something that works but looks like everyone else's page. The template shows. The fonts don't quite match your brand guidelines. The spacing feels off in a way you can't fix without breaking something else.
None of these options are wrong. They're just slow, expensive or generic. Usually two out of three.
What marketing teams actually need is simple: a custom page, built properly, on brand, live by a date they can plan around.
We built ProjectOne for founder-led businesses who need a great website without the headache. But over time, a different group started knocking on our door.
Marketing people.
It turns out the same things that make a one-page site perfect for a small business also make it perfect for a focused marketing push. Here's who we hear from most.
Marketing managers with a launch date and no dev time

You've got the campaign strategy, the creative and the budget. You don't have a developer who can give you two weeks. You need a partner who can take your brand guidelines and your brief and hand back a finished, live page.
In-house teams running multiple campaigns a year

You're not launching one thing. You're launching a product in spring, an event in summer and a big awareness push in the fall. Each one deserves its own page, and each one needs to look like it came from the same brand.
Owners and leaders launching a sub-brand

You've started something new under your main company. A new service line, a spin-off product, a community program, a separate offer for a different audience. It needs its own identity and its own home online, but it doesn't need a 20-page website. Not yet anyway.
Teams announcing something big

A press release is only as good as the place it sends people. If journalists, partners and customers click through to a buried news post on your main site, you lose the moment. A dedicated announcement page gives the news room to breathe, with the story, the visuals, the key facts and a clear next step all in one place.
Every team is different, but most requests we get fall into one of these five buckets.
1. Campaign and product launch pages

This is the classic. You're launching a product, a feature or a seasonal offer and you need one page that tells the story, shows the product and drives one action. Buy, book, sign up, download. Paid ads, email and social all point here, so every visitor arrives with the same context and sees the same message.
2. Press release and announcement pages

Funding news, a partnership, a new location, an award, a rebrand. Big news deserves more than a paragraph in a blog feed. An announcement page lets you control the narrative with headline, story, quotes, media assets and a contact for press, all designed to match the weight of the moment.
3. Sub-brand sites

A sub-brand needs to feel related to the parent brand but distinct enough to stand on its own. A single, well-designed page is often the perfect starting point. It gives the new brand a real presence, lets you test the positioning and gives you something polished to share while you figure out what comes next.
4. Coming soon pages that actually do something

Most coming soon pages are a logo, a countdown and a "stay tuned." That's a missed opportunity. A great pre-launch page builds anticipation, explains why people should care and captures interest with an email signup or a reserve button. It's the difference between "something is coming" and "I need to be first in line for this."
5. Offer pages that don't fit your main site

Sometimes you have a service, a package or a program that speaks to a completely different audience than your main website. Forcing it into your existing site confuses both audiences. A dedicated page lets you speak directly to the new group in their language, without rewriting everything else.
"On brand" gets thrown around a lot. Here's what it should mean for a campaign page.
Your typography, not a template's. Brand fonts, set properly, with the hierarchy your design team would expect.
Your colour palette, used with intent. Not just the primary colour slapped on every button. The full palette, balanced the way your guidelines describe.
Your tone of voice. Copy that sounds like your brand wrote it, not like a generic "Unlock your potential today!" headline from a template library.
Your visual system. Photography style, iconography, spacing and layout choices that feel consistent with the rest of your world.
Room for the campaign to be itself. The best campaign pages feel like part of the brand family while still having their own personality. That balance is a design skill, not a template setting.
When a page is truly on brand, your audience doesn't think about it. It just feels right. When it's not, they notice straight away, even if they can't say why.
Marketing teams sometimes worry that one page isn't "enough." In our experience, it's usually exactly right.
A single page forces clarity. You have to decide what matters most, what the visitor needs to know and what you want them to do next. That discipline is what makes landing pages convert.

Think about what a visitor actually does on a campaign page. They land. They scan. They decide whether this is for them. They take the action or they leave. That entire journey happens on one page, often in under a minute.
Extra pages don't help that journey. They distract from it.
A well-built one-page site can hold everything a campaign needs:
A strong hero with the core message and main call to action
The problem or opportunity your audience cares about
What you're offering and why it matters
Proof, like testimonials, logos, stats or press mentions
Answers to the obvious questions
One clear next step, repeated where it makes sense
That's a complete story. Nothing missing, nothing extra.

A DIY page builder. Fast and cheap. But the result often looks templated, and getting it truly on brand takes more design skill and time than most marketing teams have spare.

THREE OPTIONS. ONE RIGHT FIT.

When it comes to freelancer vs agency web design vs doing it yourself, the honest answer is that each option trades money for time and risk in a different way. DIY is cheapest in cash but most expensive in weekends, a freelancer can be great value if you pick well, and an agency brings polish at a price and pace most small businesses can't justify. If you want agency-level custom design at a fixed monthly price, live in about two weeks, there's now a fourth option worth a look.
Because every path you've looked at has left a mark.
You tried a template builder on a Sunday. By Sunday night you had three fonts you didn't choose on purpose and an urge to close the laptop forever.
You looked at Fiverr. Some portfolios looked great. Some looked like the same site with the logo swapped. It felt like a gamble.
Then you asked an agency for a quote. They were lovely. They also wanted $10k and three months.
So you did what most founders do. Nothing. The website went back on the "someday" list.
If that's you, you're not being indecisive. You're being sensible. Nobody hands you a straight comparison. So let's make one.
Here's the comparison from our own homepage. Same five questions for every option: how long, how much, is it custom, what's included, and what if you hate it.

DIY (Wix, Squarespace, Canva and friends).Timeline: live "if you find the time." Cost: your time and your sanity. Design: templates only. Copy and hosting: all on you. Guarantee: there's no refund on lost time.

Freelancer.Timeline: usually 4 to 12 weeks. Cost: roughly $3k to $8k, typically upfront. Design: custom, but it depends heavily on who you hire. Copy and hosting: rarely included. Guarantee: rarely offered.
Agency.Timeline: 3 to 6+ months. Cost: roughly $10k to $30k+, typically upfront. Design: custom, yes. Copy and hosting: almost always extra. Guarantee: rarely offered.

ProjectOne.Timeline: live in about 14 working days. Cost: $100 USD/month on the 24 plan, with no upfront lump sum. Design: always custom, never a retrofitted template. Copy and hosting: both included. Guarantee: 100% money back if you're not happy with the design direction.

We also offer the 12 plan at $199 USD/month for 12 months, for founders who'd rather pay it off faster. It includes expert copywriting, hosting for all 12 months and one revision round, with a domain included if you'd like one.
Notice what stands out. It isn't just the price. It's the risk. Three of the four options ask for a lot of money, or a lot of time, before you know whether the result will be any good.
It makes sense when:
- You're testing an idea and just need a page that exists
- Your budget is genuinely zero right now
- You actually enjoy design, and have the time to learn it properly
- You need something up this week and you'll replace it later

The catch is the part nobody puts on the pricing page. A DIY website vs web designer comparison isn't really "free vs paid." It's "your hours vs their hours." And your hours are the ones that run the business.

Most DIY sites don't fail because the builder is bad. They fail because the founder had to be copywriter, designer and conversion expert at once, after a full day of client work. The result looks like everyone else's template and quietly underperforms for years.

If you built your own and it's not pulling in enquiries, don't beat yourself up. You got something live. More on why in why your website isn't getting enquiries, and about the platform side of things in whether Wix or Squarespace is bad for SEO.
A great freelancer can be the best money you ever spend. We mean that.
Hiring a freelancer makes sense when:
- You've seen their past work and it looks like the level you want
- They have reviews or referrals from businesses like yours
- They've been clear about scope, timeline and what's included
- You have the time to manage the project and chase things when needed
The risk isn't talent. It's variance. You're betting on one person's schedule and workload staying stable for your whole project.

That's where the horror stories come from. The project that drifts from six weeks to five months. And the classic: "My web guy disappeared and I don't even know who has my domain." If that one hurts, we wrote a whole post about what to do when your web designer ghosted you.

Also watch the scope. A $3k quote often covers design and build only. Copy? You write it. Hosting? Separate. Updates? Hourly. Not shady, just how freelance pricing works, but the real cost is often higher than the invoice.
Agencies earn their fees on big, complex projects: 40-page sites, e-commerce, integrations and brand strategy.
An agency makes sense when:
- Your project is genuinely large or technically complex
- You have an internal marketing person to manage the relationship
- You have the budget to pay $10k to $30k+ upfront without it hurting
- Your timeline can stretch to three to six months, sometimes more
For a founder-led business with one to five people, most of that is overkill. You need a clear, beautiful site that says what you do, shows your work and makes it easy to get in touch.
Paying agency rates for that is like hiring three removal trucks to move one sofa. Lovely job. Painful invoice.

The DIY cost is invisible hours. Every weekend in a template builder is a weekend you didn't spend resting, selling or doing your actual work. And a homemade-looking site can quietly lose you clients who were ready to pay well.
The freelancer cost is uncertainty. If the project stalls, you're stuck with half a site and half your budget gone. If they vanish, you may lose access to your own domain.
The agency cost is cash flow and momentum. Tying up $10k or more is a big ask for a small business. So is waiting months while your current site keeps sending people away.

And there's the cost that applies to all three: the cost of waiting. While you're weighing options, the referral who Googled you and found nothing is already booking someone else. We dig into that in do I need a website if I get referrals. If you're still trying to work out what a fair budget even looks like, our breakdown of small business website cost will help.
Whoever you pick, ask these questions before you sign anything. They'll tell you more than any portfolio.
- What exactly is included: design, copywriting, development, hosting, SEO basics?
- How long will it take, and what happens if it runs late?
- How many revision rounds do I get, and how do they work?
- Who owns the site, the domain and the hosting at the end?
- What happens if I'm not happy with the design direction?
- Is payment upfront, in stages or monthly?
- Can I talk to two or three past clients?
If the answers are vague, that's your answer.

Is it cheaper to hire a freelancer or an agency?

A freelancer is usually cheaper upfront, typically around $3k to $8k compared with $10k to $30k+ for an agency. What questions should I ask a web designer before hiring them?

Ask what's included, how long it will take, how many revision rounds you get and who owns the domain and hosting afterwards. Ask what happens if you dislike the design direction, how payment works and what changes cost after launch. Clear, specific answers are the best sign you've found someone reliable.
Is it worth paying someone to build my website?

For most service businesses, yes. Your website is often the first impression a referral or search visitor gets, and a DIY site can quietly cost you well-paying clients. If you're not happy with the design direction at the First Look stage, you get a full 100% refund. No questions asked, and no hard feelings. It's there so you can try a professional, custom website without taking on the risk that usually comes with hiring a designer or an agency.

Do I need a website if I get referrals? Yes, and probably more than most businesses do. Almost every referred client looks you up before they reach out, so your website is the thing that turns a friend's recommendation into an actual phone call instead of a quiet "maybe later."
Word of mouth gets people to your door. Your website decides whether they knock.
Because they want to say yes to you. They just need a little proof first.

If your business runs on word of mouth, you already know how it goes. A past client raves about you at a barbecue. Their neighbour asks for your name. And then... sometimes they call. Sometimes they don't. You never find out which.
That's the bit that stings. Word of mouth has always worked for you. But there's a nagging voice that says, "I'm pretty sure I'm losing people I never hear about."

You're probably right. And it's not because your work isn't good enough. It's because the referral has one more step to survive before it becomes a booking, and right now that step is out of your hands.
Almost always. Think of the last time someone recommended a plumber, an accountant or a photographer to you. Did you call the number straight away? Or did you Google the name first?
Most of us do the quick check. It takes about thirty seconds and happens on a phone, usually while doing something else. The referred client is asking a few simple questions:
- Is this business real and still operating?
- Do they actually do the thing I need?
- Do they look like they'd do it well?
- Roughly what will it cost, or at least what's it like to work with them?

ONE OF A KIND, NOT ONE OF MANY.

If you built your site with an AI website builder and it isn't bringing in clients, the tool probably did its job: it gave you a website. What it couldn't give you is your website, one with a clear offer, a point of view and a path to "book a call" that feels made for the people you actually serve. The fix isn't to ditch AI. It's to add the human strategy, copy and design that turn a generic page into one that converts.
You tried it because it promised speed. Type a prompt, get a site. Twenty minutes later you had a homepage, a colour palette and a hero image of someone laughing at a laptop.
It looked okay. It also looked exactly like everyone else's.

And now it's live, and the enquiries aren't coming. So let's talk about why, what it's costing you, and what to do about it. No shame here. You were busy running a business. Trying the fast option was a completely reasonable call.
Honestly? For some things, yes.
An AI website builder is great at getting something on the screen fast: a layout, sections, a first draft of copy, fonts that don't clash. For a placeholder or a weekend test, it does the job.

Where it struggles is the part that actually wins clients. It doesn't know why people choose you over the three other bookkeepers in town. It doesn't know that your best clients are burnt-out practice owners, not startups. It doesn't know the objection every prospect raises on the first call. It fills the gaps with the most statistically likely answer, which is another way of saying the most average one.
So an AI website builder is good at making a website. Making one that sells you is a different job.
Because it was built from the middle of the internet.

AI tools learn from millions of existing sites, then produce something that looks like a reasonable blend of them. That's why so many AI generated websites share the same bones: a big headline about "transforming" something, three icon boxes, a stock photo, a testimonial slider with no testimonials in it yet, and a button that says "Get Started."
Not wrong. Just familiar. And familiar is invisible.
Your visitor has probably seen two or three competitors already. Same structure, same vague promises, same safe colour palette? Nothing to hold on to. They leave and forget whose site it was.
"My work is great. My website doesn't show it." That's the gap. Your work has personality. A template average doesn't.
Very normal. You're not bad at prompts.

The loop goes like this. The headline is fine but not quite you. You ask for a rewrite. Now it says something you don't do. You fix that, the layout shifts, and you lose the bit you liked. Three evenings later you have twelve versions and none feel finished.

The problem isn't effort. It's that AI needs direction, and direction is the hard part. To get a great result, you need to already know your positioning, your ideal client, your core message and how you want the page to flow. That's strategy. Most people use AI hoping it will give them the strategy, and it hands the question straight back.
If that sounds familiar, you might also relate to how to get a custom website built fast without doing it all yourself. Speed is great. Speed without a plan is just going in circles faster.
Not automatically. This one gets a lot of myths.

Google has been clear that it rewards helpful, original content that serves people, regardless of how it was produced. Using AI to help write or build a page is not, on its own, a problem. Publishing thin, repetitive content that says nothing new is the problem, whether a person or a tool wrote it.
Where AI built sites often trip up on search is the stuff underneath:
- Page titles and meta descriptions left on defaults or missing
- Headings used for styling instead of structure
- Vague copy that never mentions what you do and where you do it
- No FAQ content answering the questions people actually search
- Heavy images and scripts that slow the page down on phones
- No structured data (schema) to help search engines understand your business

Can Google tell a page was made with AI? Maybe. It matters less than you think. Your visitors can usually tell, though, because generic copy has a feel: smooth, polite and specific about nothing. Real people trust specifics.
And none of the issues above are AI problems. They're "nobody checked" problems.

AI search matters too now. More people ask tools like ChatGPT for recommendations, and those tools lean on clear, well-structured pages that answer questions directly. If your site is vague, it's hard for anyone, human or machine, to recommend you. We dig into this in why your business isn't showing up on Google (or ChatGPT).
A website that looks like everyone else's doesn't usually fail loudly. It fails quietly. Nobody emails to say "I didn't book because your site was bland." They just close the tab.

- Lost referrals. Someone recommends you, the prospect looks you up, and the site doesn't match the glowing review they heard. The referral cools off.

Is Wix bad for SEO? No, not on its own. Wix and Squarespace both give you the SEO basics Google needs, and plenty of small businesses rank well on them. The real problem is usually the DIY build sitting on top: vague copy, messy structure, slow pages and a site that stopped growing the day you hit publish.
You built it yourself three years ago at 11pm. It was fine. You picked a template, dropped in your logo and went to bed feeling like a legend.
Now it's not fine.

Your business has grown. Your best work isn't on there. And when you Google yourself, you find your Instagram and a competitor who is clearly worse at the job than you are. So you start wondering if the platform is the problem.
Here's the short version. The builder is rarely the villain. The build usually is.

Website builders earned a rough SEO reputation years ago. Both Wix and Squarespace have improved a lot since, and today they give you the fundamentals: editable page titles, meta descriptions, custom URLs, image alt text, automatic sitemaps, secure hosting and mobile layouts.
That means if your Wix or Squarespace site isn't showing up, the cause is probably one of these:
- Your page titles still say "Home" or your business name and nothing else
- Your headline is clever but doesn't say what you do or where you do it
- Your images are huge and slow the page down on mobile
- You have one paragraph of copy where Google needs context
- Nothing on the site has been updated since launch day
None of those are platform problems. They're DIY problems. And that's not a dig. You're running a business, not a web design studio.
Let's be fair, because they deserve it.
Website builders let millions of small business owners get online without hiring anyone. For a brand new business testing an idea, a DIY website builder is a perfectly sensible first step.
What they do well:
- Speed to launch. You can have something live in a weekend.
- Low cost to start. A monthly plan is easier to swallow than a big agency quote.
- The SEO basics are there. Titles, descriptions, alt text and sitemaps are all editable if you know where to look.
- You control it. Want to change a phone number at midnight? Go for it.
That last point is also where the trouble starts. Everything is on you, including the parts nobody told you about.
Because good SEO isn't a setting you switch on. It's the result of a well-built site with clear, useful content.
Google (and, increasingly, AI tools like ChatGPT) want to know one thing: "Is this the best result for what someone just searched?" A typical DIY build struggles on a few fronts:

Structure. Templates come with placeholder sections, filled in the order they appear rather than the order a customer needs. Headings get picked for their size, not their meaning, so Google can't tell what the page is about.

Copy. Most DIY sites say "Welcome to my website" or "Passionate about helping you thrive." Lovely. Also useless to a search engine. If you never write "bookkeeper in Chilliwack" or "personal trainer for new mums," you're asking Google to guess.
Speed. Big photos, embedded feeds, widgets added one tired evening. Each one slows things down, especially on mobile, where most people browse.
Schema. Behind-the-scenes code that tells search engines and AI tools who you are, what you offer and where. Most DIY sites don't have it, because most people have never heard of it.
If you want the full breakdown on getting found, we wrote a plain-English guide on why your business isn't showing up on Google (or ChatGPT).
Honest answer: for a small, service-based business, the difference between Squarespace SEO and Wix SEO is much smaller than the difference between a well-built site and a rushed one.
Switching from one DIY website builder to another without changing the copy, structure and strategy is like repainting a car with a flat tyre. Looks fresher. Still not going anywhere.
A website that "sort of works" feels free because you already paid for it. It isn't.
Lost enquiries. Someone looks you up, lands on a site that feels out of date and quietly books someone else. You never hear about it. The cost is invisible.

Lower prices. When your website looks like a side hustle, people expect side hustle rates. It's hard to charge premium prices from a template you picked in a hurry. We go deeper on this in Embarrassed by Your Website?
Your evenings. Every fix is another late night of dragging boxes around and watching tutorials.
Visibility. If Google doesn't understand your site, you rely on referrals and social media to fill the calendar. Both are great. Neither should be your only option.
Add those up and the "cheap" website starts looking pretty expensive.

- Your services, prices or location have changed and the site hasn't caught up
- Your site looks broken or cramped on your own phone

- Nobody ever fills in your contact form

Switch to a custom website if the problem is bigger than a few settings. If your positioning has changed, your site doesn't reflect the quality of your work, or you've patched it so many times it feels like a garden shed held together with tape, starting fresh is often faster than fixing.

"How do I make my business look professional online?" If you typed that into Google at 10pm, here's the answer: the fastest fix is a clear, custom website that matches the quality of your actual work. Not more posting. Not another template. One focused site with sharp copy, clean design and an obvious next step, so people trust you before they ever pick up the phone.
That's the short answer. Here's the longer, kinder one.
You finish a great call. The client is keen. They ask, "Do you have a website?"
And there's a tiny pause.
You send the link anyway. Then you add, "It's a bit out of date," before they've even opened it. Maybe you say, "Honestly, just check my Instagram."
Sound familiar? You're in good company. Most of the founders we talk to say some version of the same thing: "My work is great. My website makes me look like a hobby."

That gap between how good you are and how good you look online is exhausting. It chips away at your confidence. It makes you hesitate before sharing your own business. And it's not your fault. You were busy doing the work, not designing a website.
Short version: your business grew and your website didn't.

Most small business websites are built at a very specific moment. Usually the week you launched, usually late at night, usually on a DIY builder with a template that looked fine at the time. Or a friend of a friend built it at friends-and-family rates. Or you paid someone on Fiverr and crossed your fingers.

Then life happened. You got better at what you do. Your prices went up. Your clients got bigger. Your offer changed twice. And the website sat there, frozen in time, like a school photo you can't take down.
A few common culprits:
- Template sameness. Your site looks like hundreds of others because it literally is hundreds of others with a new logo.
- Copy written in a hurry. It says what you do, sort of, but not who it's for or why you're the right choice.
- Old photos (or no photos). Blurry phone shots, stock images of people shaking hands, or your headshot from 2017.
- It breaks on phones. Most people will see your site on their phone first. If the text is tiny and the buttons are fiddly, it reads as "not quite legit."
- It's slow. Plugins, giant images and years of bolted-on bits make it drag.

None of this means you did a bad job. It means you built a website for the business you had, not the business you run now. If you've been wondering whether the builder itself is the problem, we broke that down honestly in Is Wix or Squarespace Bad for SEO?.
You probably already know. But if you want a gut check, run through this list. Open your site on your phone, pretend you're a stranger, and be brutally honest.
- You'd rather send people to your Instagram than your website
- The first thing people see is a vague headline like "Welcome to our website"
- You can't tell who the business is for within five seconds
- There's no clear button telling people what to do next
- Your prices, services or location have changed and the site hasn't
- It takes more than a few seconds to load on mobile data
- You apologise for it before you share it
If you ticked three or more, it's not a "someday" job. It's quietly working against you right now.
Because your website is often the first meeting, and you're not in the room.

People make snap judgements. It's not fair, but it's human. Before a potential client reads a single word about your experience, they've already absorbed the look and feel of your site and decided whether you seem trustworthy, current and worth the money.
For a founder-led business, your website is the storefront, the brochure and the handshake all at once.

And here's the part people forget: even referrals check you out. Someone hears your name from a friend, then Googles you before calling. If what they find feels dated or thin, that warm introduction cools off quietly. You never hear about it. We wrote a whole post on this, Do I Need a Website If All My Clients Come From Referrals?, because it happens far more than most owners realise.
This is where it stops being about vanity and starts being about money.
You're losing clients you never hear about. Nobody emails to say, "I was going to hire you, but your website put me off." They just close the tab and book someone who looked more put together.

You're charging less than you should. Perception sets price. If your site says "side hustle," clients mentally file you in the budget bracket and push back on your quotes. A professional presence gives you permission to charge what your work is worth, and makes it far easier for clients to say yes.
You're attracting the wrong fit. A vague, dated site tends to pull in bargain hunters and tyre kickers. A clear, confident one attracts people who value quality and are ready to invest.

You're working harder to stay visible. When the website can't close the deal, you compensate. More posts. More DMs. More explaining. That treadmill is tiring, and it's one reason so many owners want to get clients without relying on Instagram.
It's costing you confidence. When you're proud of your site, you share it everywhere. When you're not, you hide it. That hesitation adds up.
Quick wins you can do this week, before any bigger website redesign:
- Rewrite your headline. Say what you do, who it's for and the result. "Kitchen renovations for busy families in the Fraser Valley" beats "Quality you can trust" every time.
- Add one clear call to action. Pick the single thing you want people to do (book a call, request a quote) and make that button obvious.
- Swap your photos. Even well-lit phone photos of you and your real work beat generic stock.
- Fix your contact details. Make sure your email, phone and service area are current and easy to find.
- Add proof. Two or three genuine client reviews, with names, do a lot of work for trust.
These help. But if the foundations are shaky (the template, the structure, the mobile layout, the speed), patching only gets you so far. At some point you're putting new paint on a wobbly fence.
Trust isn't built with one flashy feature. It's built with a lot of small signals that all say the same thing: "This person is legit and knows what they're doing."
The big ones:
- Clarity. People trust what they understand. Plain language, a clear offer and a simple layout beat clever wordplay every time.
- Consistency. Your brand should look and sound the same everywhere. Mismatched logos and colours feel careless, even when you're not.
- Real proof. Reviews, before and after shots, recognisable client names, credentials. Show, don't tell.
This is what professional website design really is. Not fancy animations. Clear thinking, presented beautifully.
Yes, and this is the bit we get most excited about.

When your online presence finally matches the quality of your work, a few things tend to shift. Clients arrive already sold on your expertise, so the first call is less about convincing and more about planning. Price objections soften because you look like the premium option. And you feel different quoting your rates, because you're not silently apologising for your website in the background.
We can't promise a specific number. Nobody honest can. But a website you're proud of changes how you show up, and how you're perceived.
The homepage line we keep coming back to says it best: because the small guys deserve great design too.
Here's the honest comparison.

It's rarely villainy. Most ghosting comes from a few boring, very human reasons:

Your domain is your shopfront sign and phone number rolled into one. Check it first.
- Go to the free ICANN lookup tool at lookup.icann.org, or any reputable WHOIS lookup, and type in your domain.
- Look for three things: the registrar (the company the domain is registered through), the expiry date, and the registrant (the owner on record).
- Don't panic if the owner shows as "privacy protected" or a proxy service. That's normal. The registrar still knows who the account holder is.
- Search your email for receipts from that registrar. If you find an invoice in your name, you may already own it and just need to reset the password.
If the domain was registered in your name or your business name, brilliant. Log in, change the password, turn on two-factor authentication and set it to auto-renew.
If it's registered to the designer, keep reading.
First, ask. In writing. Politely. Something like: "Please transfer the domain to my account, or send me the authorisation code, by [date]." Ghosting is often avoidance, not malice.
If that deadline passes, contact the registrar's support team directly. Explain that the domain was registered on your behalf for your business, and have your proof ready:
- Invoices or receipts showing you paid for the domain or the project that included it
- Your contract or written agreement, if you have one
- Emails or messages where the designer confirms the domain is for your business
- Your business registration documents and matching ID

Every registrar has its own process, so be patient and persistent. Once you regain control, you'll typically need to unlock the domain and get an authorisation (EPP) code before moving it to a registrar account in your own name. Some registrars apply a temporary transfer lock after ownership details change, so don't be alarmed if there's a short wait.

If the domain is valuable to your business and nobody's cooperating, check your contract and talk to a professional about your options. We're website people, not lawyers, and this is the moment for proper advice.
Work out where the site is hosted. Your WHOIS lookup shows the nameservers, which often hint at the host. Then go down this list:

- Business email. If your email runs on your domain, find out who's the admin on your email provider account. This one matters more than the website.
- Shared passwords. Change any password you ever sent the designer: social accounts, Google Business Profile, analytics, payment tools.
- Your content. Copy every word of text and download every image from the live or staging site while you can. The Wayback Machine at web.archive.org may also hold older snapshots.

Business not showing up on Google? It's usually because Google can't find your website, can't understand what you do, or doesn't trust it enough yet to show it. The fix isn't a secret trick: it's a clear, fast website with the right titles, schema and FAQs, plus a Google Business Profile, so both search engines and AI tools know exactly who you are and who you help.
You typed your own business name into Google. Scrolled.
Nothing. Or worse, a competitor.
That little sinking feeling? Very common. And very fixable.

Let's start with the good news. You haven't done anything wrong. Most small business owners never got a proper handover on how search works. You were busy doing the actual work: fixing the roof, balancing the books, coaching the client, shooting the wedding.

Meanwhile, your website was quietly built on a template, launched in a hurry, or handed over by someone who has since vanished. (If that last one sounds familiar, we wrote about what to do when your web designer ghosts you.)

Google isn't a phone book. It doesn't list every business by default. It sends out crawlers to find pages, tries to understand them, then decides which ones are worth showing for each search. If any of those three steps breaks, you're invisible.
So when your business is not showing up on Google, it almost always comes down to one of three problems:
- Google hasn't found your site yet
- Google found it but can't tell what you do or where you do it
- Google understands it but trusts other sites more
Here's a two-second test. Go to Google and type `site:yourdomain.com` (swap in your actual web address). If nothing comes back, Google hasn't indexed your site at all.
Common reasons:
- The site is brand new and Google hasn't crawled it yet
- A setting on your website builder is telling search engines to stay away
- There's no sitemap, so Google has no map of what to crawl

The fix here is refreshingly boring. Set up Google Search Console (it's free), verify your domain, and submit your sitemap. That's you politely telling Google, "Hi, I exist, here's where everything is."
When someone searches "bookkeeper near me" or "landscaper in Kelowna," Google usually shows a map with three local businesses before any regular results.
Those listings come from Google Business Profile, not your website. If you haven't claimed and verified a profile, you won't appear there, full stop.
A few quick wins for local SEO:
- Claim and verify your Google Business Profile
- Pick the most accurate primary category (be specific: "Interior designer," not just "Designer")
- Keep your business name, address and phone number identical everywhere they appear online
- Ask happy clients for reviews, and reply to them

Your Google Business Profile and your website work as a team. Google checks one against the other. A profile that links to a slow, vague or outdated website is a bit like a great first impression followed by an awkward silence.
This is the big one. Plenty of websites are indexed but still invisible, because Google can't work out what they're about.
Google reads your page the way a very literal visitor would. It looks at:
- Your page title (the blue link text in search results)
- Your meta description (the short summary underneath)
- Your headings and the words in them
- Whether your copy clearly names your service and your location
If your page title is "Home" and your headline is a vibe rather than a sentence, you're asking Google to guess.

The fix for small business SEO is clarity. Say what you do, who it's for and where you do it, in words your clients actually type. "Residential landscaping in Chilliwack" beats "Transforming outdoor dreams" every single time.
Clear copy also wins enquiries. If people find you but don't reach out, our post on why your website is not getting enquiries digs into that side.
Most people browse on their phone. Google knows this, so it looks at the mobile version of your site first when deciding how to rank it.
Common culprits on DIY and template sites:
- Huge, uncompressed images straight off a camera
- Layouts that were designed on a desktop and squished onto mobile as an afterthought
If you're on one of the big template platforms and wondering whether it's holding you back, have a read of is Wix or Squarespace bad for SEO.

Here's the newer twist. More people now skip the search results and just ask. "Who's a good bookkeeper for trades businesses in BC?" goes into ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity or Google's own AI answers, and out comes a short list.
Being on that list is called AEO, or answer engine optimisation. It's SEO's younger sibling, and it cares about slightly different things.
AI tools pull from websites they can read easily and trust. They love:
- Clear, direct answers to real questions (hello, FAQs)
- Plain statements of who you are, what you do and where
- Structured data (schema) that labels your business details
- Consistent information across your website, Google Business Profile and directories
If your site is mostly images and clever taglines, an AI tool has nothing to quote. The good news: what helps AI search visibility also helps humans. Clear answers, honest detail, no fluff.

When your business is not showing up on Google, you don't get a notification. There's no email saying "Seven people looked for a kitchen renovator in your town today and found someone else." The cost is silent.
Here's what it tends to look like in real life:

- More hustle. You end up posting on social every day just to stay visible, because your website isn't doing any of the heavy lifting.
- Competing on price. When people can't see your quality, they compare you on the one thing they can see: cost.

Your work might be brilliant. But if people can't find it, Google can't vouch for it, and AI can't describe it, the brilliance stays a well-kept secret. For more on this, see why your service-based business needs one website that actually works.
Right. Enough about the problem. Here's the fix. You don't need to become an SEO expert. You need the fundamentals done properly, once.

- Write a unique page title with your main service and location in it
- Write a meta description that says what you do and why someone should click
- Use one clear headline that names your service in plain words
- Add descriptive alt text to your images
- Compress images and keep the page fast on mobile
- Add schema markup for your business (more on this below)
- Include an FAQ section that answers the questions clients actually ask you
- Add an llms.txt file so AI tools get a clean summary of your business
- Claim, verify and fill out your Google Business Profile
- Keep your name, address and phone number consistent everywhere
- Collect reviews, steadily, from real clients
Schema sounds technical. It's actually quite simple.

It's a bit of hidden code on your website that labels information for search engines and AI tools. Instead of Google reading "Open Monday to Friday, 8 to 5" and guessing what it means, schema says, "These are the business hours." Same for your business name, location, services and FAQs.
Schema won't magically push you to the top of Google. It removes the guesswork, so your details are more likely to show up correctly, in search and in AI answers.

This one is newer. An llms.txt file is a short, plain text summary of your website, written specifically for AI tools like ChatGPT. It sits on your site and says, in effect, "Here's who we are, here's what we do, here are the important pages."

Is it a guaranteed ticket into AI recommendations? No. Nobody can honestly promise that. But it's a small, low-effort way to make your business easier for AI tools to read and summarise accurately, and it's quickly becoming part of good AEO housekeeping.

Small business website conversion comes down to one simple test. Can a stranger land on your homepage, on their phone, and answer these three questions in about five seconds?

- Is it for someone like me?
- What should I do next?

If any of those answers are fuzzy, people bounce. Not because they don't need you. Because figuring you out feels like homework. The good news? Clarity is fixable. Below are the seven most common reasons a website is not getting enquiries, each with a quick fix you can start on today.
This is the big one. Your homepage headline is the most valuable real estate you own online, and it's often spent on something like "Welcome to Smith & Co" or "Passion. Quality. Excellence."
Lovely words. Zero information.
If your headline could belong to a dentist, a law firm or a bakery, it's not doing its job.

Quick fix: rewrite your headline so it names the outcome you deliver and the person you deliver it for. "Landscape design for Fraser Valley homeowners who want a backyard they actually use" beats "Creating beautiful spaces" every single time.
Many service businesses list everything they could possibly do. Twelve services, four packages, a mission statement. The thing most clients actually want is buried, and confused people don't buy.

Quick fix: pick your ONE core offer, the thing most of your best clients come to you for, and make it the star. Explain what's included, roughly how it works (three or four simple steps is perfect) and what someone gets at the end. If you're comfortable sharing pricing, show a starting point.

Plenty of websites hide the call to action. A single "Contact" link tucked in the navigation. A button labelled "Submit" that sounds about as inviting as a tax return. If people have to hunt for the next step, most won't bother.

Quick fix: decide on one primary action (book a call, request a quote, check availability) and repeat it. Put a clear button in the hero, again after you explain your offer, and again at the end. Use words that describe what happens next, like "Book a free 15-minute call" or "Get your quote." Keep your form short too. Name, email, one or two questions.

Your past clients love you. But on your website? Not a single review, no photos of real work. Just you saying you're great. Without proof, the safest choice for a stranger is to do nothing. When a referral checks you out and finds a thin site, that warm lead goes cold quietly.

Quick fix: gather three to five genuine testimonials and put them near your call to action, not hidden on a separate page. Add real photos of your work, your team or your space. Specific beats vague. "Sarah redesigned our kitchen in six weeks and stayed on budget" lands harder than "Great service!"

Most people browse on their phone. That's not a hot take, it's just Tuesday. Yet plenty of small business sites were never properly checked on one. Tiny text, cramped buttons, slow images. People won't pinch and zoom their way to your contact form. They'll tap the next Google result.
Quick fix: open your own website on your phone, on mobile data, not Wi-Fi. Time how long it takes to load. Compress oversized images and make sure your main button is easy to tap.
Generic copy is a silent conversion killer. "We are committed to providing high-quality solutions tailored to your needs." Every business says it, so it means nothing.
Plenty of people tried AI, went in circles and ended up sounding exactly like their competitors. We've written more about that in why AI-built websites often don't win clients. People hire people.
Quick fix: write the way you talk to clients on the phone. Use the words your clients use to describe their problem. Your personality is a genuine differentiator.

Quick fix: make sure every page has a clear title and description that includes what you do and where you do it. Claim your Google Business Profile. More in our guide on why your business isn't showing up on Google.

A website that doesn't convert isn't a neutral asset. It's a leak.

A website isn't a nice-to-have anymore. For most service-based businesses, it's the very first impression a potential client gets, and it happens before they ever call, email, or DM you. If that first impression is a DIY builder from three years ago, a template that looks like everyone else's, or no website at all, you're losing trust before the conversation even starts.
This is the exact gap ProjectOne was built to close.

Most service-based business owners we talk to never planned to go years without a proper website. It just happened. Life got busy. Referrals kept the phone ringing, so the website felt optional. Then one day a prospective client Googles the business, finds nothing worth clicking, and quietly moves on to a competitor who looked more legitimate.
Sound familiar? You're not alone. Some of the things we hear on almost every discovery call:
- "The last agency used a template, and it shows."
- "I don't have time to figure out Wix, Squarespace, or whatever else is out there."
- "It looked fine on my laptop, but I opened it on my phone and cringed."
- "I've been burned by a freelancer before and I'm gun-shy."
- "WordPress keeps breaking and I have no idea why."
None of that means you're bad at running a business. It means building a website was never supposed to be your job in the first place.
Here's the part nobody says plainly enough: your website is doing a job whether you like it or not. Right now, it's either quietly building trust or quietly chipping away at it.

When your brand perception finally matches the quality of what you actually deliver, everything shifts. Your confidence goes up. Your pricing power goes up. Your credibility with the exact clients you want to attract goes up. A professional, custom-designed site tells a visitor in about three seconds that this is a business worth reaching out to.

A DIY site, even a decent one, rarely pulls that off. Templates are built to work for a thousand different businesses at once, which means they're built to be generic. Your business isn't generic. Your website shouldn't be either.

ProjectOne. Live in 14 days. $100 USD per month. Always custom. Copy and hosting included. Backed by a 100% money-back guarantee.
